title: The half plot
brief:
Write a complete story for a general adult audience about two strangers assigned to share a community garden plot for one growing season. Ada wants room for the beans her father used to grow. Kit plans to raise flowers for a sibling's August wedding and can visit only on Wednesday evenings. They have a single locker key, a shared path along the sunny edge, and a volunteer coordinator who checks plots once a month. Use scenes at three points in the season. Give both gardeners a say in how the plot changes, and bring the story to a close when Kit comes to cut the flowers.

Aim for 1,200 to 1,800 words. Return the complete original work directly in your answer. Do not sign or identify yourself. Do not use tools.

c153f46da9fd0d9f.text:
The first thing Ada and Kit grew together was a quarrel over six inches.

On the first Wednesday in May, Ada drove a stake into the ground and Kit said, “That’s the path.”

“It’s the edge of the path.”

“My foot’s on it.”

Ada looked down. Kit had remarkably long shoes. She pulled up the stake.

They had met nine minutes earlier, when Leon, the volunteer coordinator, assigned them plot fourteen for the season. Now he was working his way down the row, handing out locker keys on rings made of bent curtain hooks. The garden had once been a bowling green. A wall shaded the east end, and on the sunny west edge of their plot a narrow path served both them and the woman who grew onions next door.

“My dad grew these up the whole side of his garage,” Ada said. She opened the tobacco tin in her pocket. Inside were forty or fifty beans, almost black, each with a little cream dash that looked painted on. “I was hoping for two rows.”

Kit tipped six packets of flower seed out of a coat pocket. “My brother’s getting married in August. I told him I’d do the tables.”

“How many?”

“I asked him that after I said yes. Twelve.”

Leon came back with their key. There was one locker for each plot and one key for each locker. He did his rounds the first Wednesday of every month, he told them. If they wanted help in between, his number was on the shed.

“Which of you wants to keep this?”

“Kit,” Ada said, at the same time Kit said, “Ada.”

“I can only come Wednesday evenings,” Kit explained. “I sew alterations at the department store. Wednesday we close at five, and Sunday I have my brother’s kids. If there’s a nice Sunday in June you’ll be standing here wanting a hoe and I’ll be watching a seven-year-old swallow pool water.”

Ada took the key. “I’m usually home by six.”

“Usually is what worries me.”

They stood over the bare ground. Ada had imagined kneeling here alone, dropping the beans into holes the depth of her first knuckle, as her father had shown her when they were both young enough to get down on their knees without thinking about it. This person in the long shoes had imagined twelve tables.

“Across the north end,” Kit said. “Could you put the beans there? The sun would still get to the flowers. I could leave a gap through the middle so you could get to them.”

Ada looked at the length of the bed. “If you give me three feet at that end, I can make a tent of the poles. You could plant right up to it on the south side.”

Kit measured three feet with a yellow dressmaker’s tape. Ada set the stake again.

They sowed two kinds of zinnia and some cosmos, putting the other packets away for another year. Ada planted sixteen beans. While Kit fetched water she found herself counting them again, as if somebody might later require an accounting for the ones she had left in the tin.

At the gate she showed Kit the little grocery opposite, where the owner let her leave things for her daughter. They went in to ask if he would hold their key on Wednesdays. He considered the curtain hook.

“In an envelope,” he said. “Last thing I need is another object nobody knows the purpose of.”

Kit borrowed his pen and wrote PLOT FOURTEEN in the square, clear capitals of someone accustomed to chalking marks on expensive cloth.

* * *

On the first Wednesday in July, Ada arrived carrying string and found a bicycle lying in the onions. Its owner, Leon’s ten-year-old daughter, stood beside it with a green smear down one shin. The onion grower was straightening the bent tops, and Kit was unwinding a bean runner from a bicycle pedal.

“You all right?” Ada asked the girl.

“I was walking it,” she said fiercely.

“She was,” Kit said. “The pedal caught.”

Since May the bean tent had become a house. Runners went up the poles, met at the top, and came down again with energy to spare. The cosmos along the path had also done well. Together they had narrowed the passage to a slot you could negotiate sideways, provided nothing about you stuck out.

Leon took hold of the handlebars. “I need a wheelbarrow to get through here by the time I finish my rounds.”

Ada lifted a hanging runner so the girl could wheel her bike away. Under its leaves dangled the first beans long enough to pick. Her father used to send her home with a bread bag full, whether she wanted them or not. She had been looking forward to being the person who did the sending.

“I can tie these back,” she said.

“You tied them back last week.” Kit wiped bicycle grease onto a scrap of lining silk. “I’ll take out this row of cosmos. Can you move that end pole in?”

“There are four plants on it.”

“And there are flowers on mine.”

They regarded the path. From the grocery across the road came the clank of the shutters being raised for evening trade.

“I watered those flowers through eleven days without rain,” Ada said. Hearing it aloud, she realized she had been saving it up.

Kit sat back on their heels. “I know how often you’re here. Every time I pick up the key he tells me.”

“I didn’t ask him to.”

“I know that too.” Kit folded the silk over the greasy spot. “I thought we’d agreed you liked watering. You said it was the best part of your day.”

“It was May when I said that.”

A laugh got out of Kit, and after a moment Ada joined in. It had been a beautiful May. You could have got her to agree to anything.

Kit took the tape from around their neck and measured the width of the path farther down. They drew a line in the dirt with the point of the sewing scissors. “If we clear up to here, he’ll get his barrow through. What about those bean plants that run up together? Could we lead the tops across to the next pole before we shift this one?”

Ada felt along the stems. Two were still supple. The other two had wound themselves together so tightly she could barely get a finger between them.

“Give me the scissors,” she said.

She cut the two thick stems low. Kit worked the severed vines loose while Ada eased the remaining pair, still attached to their pole, toward the middle of the tent. Then they lifted six cosmos with slabs of earth around their roots. The onion grower took three for her front steps. The others went in the gap through the middle of the plot, which Ada decided she could give up now that she could reach the beans from the path.

Leon came back pushing a barrow with his daughter sitting in it like a queen. She held her arms tight against her sides as they passed. A cosmos leaf brushed her elbow. Nothing broke.

“I can soak everything properly on Wednesdays,” Kit said. “And put down that leaf mulch Leon’s been trying to give away. Would twice a week besides that do it?”

“Most weeks. If we get another hot spell I’ll ring you and complain.”

“Please do. I spend all day with people who tell me a jacket fits beautifully and then bring it back.”

Before they left, Ada divided the beans from the cut vines into two small handfuls. Kit ate one raw and pronounced it furry. Ada told them to get a pan of water boiling first, for God’s sake.

* * *

On the third Wednesday in August, Kit came to cut the flowers wearing good gray trousers and carrying two white buckets from the store’s cleaning cupboard. Ada had unlocked the locker and put the snips out. The first zinnias were fading, but the plants they had cut back in July had branched, and now the bed was full of heads in shades of orange and rose. Two of the transplanted cosmos had lived. Their white flowers hung out over the zinnias on stems so fine they seemed to have arrived separately and settled there.

“Still twelve tables?” Ada asked.

“Eleven. My brother discovered he had seated our dead aunt. He’d worked from the invitation list for his first wedding.”

Ada counted out twelve bunches anyway. “One for the kitchen. Somebody always gets stuck in there.”

They cut in the long evening light, stripping the lower leaves so they wouldn’t foul the water. Halfway through, Kit stopped with the snips open.

“It looks a bit awful where we’ve been.”

“It does,” Ada said. A whole summer of coming through the gate and looking first for color, and now she could see the wall. “Keep going. You promised him flowers.”

Kit cut the last long zinnia, a pink one with a crooked neck that would hang nicely over the lip of a jug. Ada held the buckets steady while Kit fitted it in among the others.

Along the moved pole hung three dry pods Ada had saved for seed. She broke one open. The beans lay in their hollows, black with cream dashes, as clean as if her father had just rubbed them on his shirt.

Kit held out a hand. “Could I have a couple? My niece has decided the wedding flowers are hers to grow next year. I’d like something of my own.”

Ada tipped the whole pod into Kit’s palm. Kit found the key envelope in the locker and slipped the beans inside, folding the flap twice.

At the gate each took a bucket. Even so, water slopped onto Kit’s good trousers. They waited for a gap in traffic, then carried the flowers across the road together. Inside the grocery the owner moved his pyramid of oranges so they could set the buckets on his counter while Kit fetched the car.

“Which one’s mine?” he asked.

Ada looked at Kit. Kit lifted the crooked pink zinnia out of the wedding flowers and laid it across his till.

3c23a14e6a063ed0.text:
On the first Wednesday in May, Ada arrived at Plot 19 with six bean poles and found a stranger measuring it in shoes.

“Eleven and a half,” the stranger said, completing a heel-to-toe traverse of the bed. “I was promised twelve.”

“Feet?”

“Mine, apparently.”

Ada set down her poles. The stranger stepped off the soil and put out a hand. Their name was Kit. They had brought a paper bag from the hardware store and a drawing on the back of an envelope. The drawing showed three broad bands of flowers, with a little square at the bottom labeled BUCKET.

“My sister’s getting married in August,” Kit said. “I told her I could do the tables.”

“How many tables?”

“Six when I told her.”

Ada took a small brown envelope from her coat pocket. She had written the year on it in pencil. Inside were the last beans she’d shelled with her father at his kitchen table. He had made her pick through the pile twice because she kept letting the split ones go into the envelope. She’d found another split one that morning and put it back with the others. It had seemed a poor day to start throwing things away.

“I need room for these,” she said.

Maribel, the volunteer coordinator, came through the gate with a clipboard and a key on a green plastic coil. She was giving the new plot holders their May check. The strip of packed earth along the south edge, she told them, was their shared path. It had to stay clear from the gate to the water tap. She handed Ada the key, which opened the tool locker beside the gate.

“One per plot. I come round once a month, so put both your names on the board if you need me to call.”

Ada slipped the coil over her wrist. Kit looked at it.

“I can only come Wednesday evenings,” they said. “I close the bakery the other nights. Could you leave that somewhere I can get it?”

Ada had already imagined bringing the key home and hanging it on the hook where she kept her spare. She looked at the locker. Its feet stood on two cinder blocks. Kit crouched and reached into the back of one, up to the wrist.

“Can you see my hand?”

Ada bent down. “I can see your watch.”

Kit took off the watch and tried again. They agreed on the block.

With a stick, Ada drew a line down the middle of the bed, dividing it into two rectangles that each met the path. She wanted her bean poles at the front of hers. The path would give her somewhere firm to stand while she picked, and she could see the pods with the light behind them. Her father used to come in from picking with green crescents on his thumbnail.

Kit followed the line of the poles with their eyes. “How tall do those get?”

“As tall as the poles, then they look for something else.”

“Could we keep this corner open?” Kit pointed to the end nearest the tap. “I’ll be coming in with a bucket after work. I’d like to get it all the way into the bed.”

Ada shifted the line a shoe’s width at the front. Kit redrew the flower bands to fit and gave Ada the stick so she could mark the first bean hole. By the time the light went, Kit had shaken out the zinnia seeds and folded the empty packet into a square small enough to fit behind their watch. Ada planted nine beans and kept three in the envelope.

* * *

At the July check, Maribel laid her clipboard flat on the path. A bean runner had found the wire fence on the other side and crossed at about the height of her knee. She lifted it with the end of her pen.

“This comes down tonight,” she said. “Somebody’s going to carry a watering can straight through it.”

Ada fetched the scissors. She had tucked the runner back into the poles the previous weekend. When she cut it, the loose end stayed in the air a moment, hooked to itself, before falling.

Kit let themselves in just after seven, still wearing a white bakery shirt with a streak of something dark at the elbow. Ada could tell when they saw the gap in the flowers. They set their bag down before they said anything.

“Where are the cosmos?”

“By the tap.”

Three drooping plants stood in a row at the edge of the bucket space. Ada had moved them on Sunday. Their roots had held almost no soil, and she’d carried each plant across the bed with both hands cupped around a little rag of dirt.

“They were leaning into the beans,” she said. “They’d have snapped.”

Kit pressed one finger into the ground beside a stem. “I put stakes in the locker for them.”

Ada had seen the stakes. She had taken them for kindling left by the last plot holder.

Kit picked up the bucket and tried to set it beside the tap. There was room for the base if they tipped it, though the handle caught a stem. They lifted it out again. Ada could hear water running in the next plot, splashing against the hollow sides of somebody else’s can.

“I can move them back,” she said.

Kit glanced at the strip where the cosmos had been. The beans cast a shadow across it and over the first row of zinnias. Some of the zinnias had grown sideways toward the path. Kit slid a palm beneath one of the stems. A bud the size of a shirt button rested against their finger.

“I think the poles need to go to the back,” they said.

Ada looked up at the bean leaves, which were so thick now she could stand behind them and be quite alone. “The roots are at the front.”

“Can we leave the roots there?”

They stood for a while looking from the bases of the plants to the far corners of the bed. Kit took two of the thin stakes from the locker and held them out at an angle. Ada could see how the vines might go up that way, with a low section at the front and the height at the back. She put a hand around one of her poles and felt it give. Several runners wound around it together. One had already wound twice around its neighbor.

“We’d have to cut some,” she said.

Kit put the stakes down.

Ada found the stems she could follow cleanly from the ground to the first fork. She gave those to Kit to hold while she worked loose the twine. There were two she couldn’t free. She cut them low, with her thumb over the place where the blades met, then carried the poles to the back and pushed them in. They used Kit’s stakes to keep the vines off the soil on the way up. By the time they tied the last knot, Ada had dirt down the front of her shirt and Kit’s white sleeve was green.

Kit pinched a spent bloom from one of the cosmos and carried the plant to the sunny space the poles had vacated. They dug the other two holes wide enough to take a shovelful of earth with each plant. When the bucket fitted at the end again, Kit filled it and watered the transplants slowly. Ada held each stem upright while the ground settled around it.

“How many tables now?” Ada asked.

“Eight. My sister says the cousins can sit together, which is how we got nine last week.”

Ada washed the scissors under the tap. “Bring nine jars.”

* * *

On the Wednesday before the wedding, Kit came through the gate carrying a cardboard wine box with nine jars packed into it. Ada was sitting on the locker step, shelling a pod she’d left too long. She slid over so Kit could reach the cinder block. The green coil had bleached almost white on the side that stuck out into the sun.

At the back of the bed, the beans had reached the tops of the poles again. Ada had left a few pods to dry for seed. She picked the tender ones by reaching between the slanted stakes, and sometimes she had to get down on both knees. She had brought a shallow bowl for the evening’s picking. Kit looked into it and chose a bean with a curl at one end.

“Can I eat it like this?”

“That’s how I test them.”

Kit bit into it. Ada waited for them to say what it tasted like. Her father had always said the younger ones tasted of peas. She remembered disagreeing with him, though she could no longer remember what she’d thought they tasted of instead.

Kit finished the bean and opened the locker for the shears.

The zinnias in the sunny strip stood higher than Kit’s waist. They had bloomed in brick red and pale yellow and a pink that Kit’s sister had described, when shown a photograph, as exactly the color of the bathroom she’d spent two years trying to get her landlord to repaint. Kit had brought the photograph with that message still beneath it. Ada had laughed hard enough to have to sit down.

Now Kit filled the bucket at the tap, set it in its square, and took hold of the tallest pink stem. They followed it down to a pair of leaves. At the click of the shears, Ada put out her hand, and Kit gave her the flower. She stripped the leaves that would sit below the water and lowered the stem into the bucket. They worked down the row like that. Kit turned each stem to see where the next bud was coming, and Ada made room in the bucket. There were enough long stems for all the jars. Kit took some of the cosmos last, including a white one from the plant that had wilted worst in July. They left it a flower with a yellow center already busy with a bee.

When the light began to go, Kit set the jars along the path and divided the stems among them. The pink flowers went in every jar. The last one had a bend halfway up that put its bloom close to the glass.

“That one’s my sister’s,” Kit said, and fitted the jar into the middle of the box.

Ada waited while Kit took the shears back. She heard the locker shut and the little scrape of the key going into the block.

Kit lifted the box. The flowers brushed their chin. Ada walked ahead to hold the gate, with the bowl of beans tucked against her hip. At the sidewalk Kit stopped to shift their grip, and Ada steadied the box from underneath until they had it. Then Kit carried the flowers out into the last of the light.
